title: Administrative Rule-Making — Need, Limits and Classification

content.overview: Limits on administrative rule-making include the doctrine against excessive delegation, consistency with the parent Act and the Constitution, compliance with mandatory procedure (publication, consultation where required), and fundamental-rights constraints.
content.glance: Test the rule for (1) source and excessive delegation, (2) consistency with parent Act and Constitution, (3) mandatory procedure, and (4) fundamental-rights compliance.
content.study: A rule may fail because the parent delegation is excessive, because the rule contradicts the parent Act, because mandatory laying or publication requirements were ignored, or because the rule violates fundamental rights or equality. Procedural ultra vires and substantive ultra vires are distinct pathways. Current-law framing: ground the analysis in the parent Act and Constitution. Do not treat BSA 2023 as the source of this doctrine.

sections.heading: Excessive Delegation
sections.body: Abdication of essential legislative function voids the delegation.

sections.heading: Substantive Ultra Vires
sections.body: Rules inconsistent with the parent Act or Constitution are void.

sections.heading: Procedural Ultra Vires
sections.body: Failure of mandatory publication, consultation or laying requirements can invalidate rules.

sections.heading: Fundamental Rights
sections.body: Subordinate legislation must respect Part III of the Constitution.

sections.heading: Remedies
sections.body: Rules may be quashed under Articles 226/32; severability may save valid parts.

examples.title: Rule beyond parent Act
examples.body: A rule imposes a burden not authorised by the parent statute. Substantive ultra vires is made out.

examples.title: Mandatory publication skipped
examples.body: A statute requires publication before a rule takes effect; publication is omitted. Procedural ultra vires may invalidate the rule.

hypotheticals.question: Is the Constitution irrelevant to rules if the parent Act is satisfied?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Rules must also comply with the Constitution including fundamental rights.

hypotheticals.question: Does any procedural slip void a rule?
hypotheticals.analysis: Only mandatory procedural requirements have nullifying effect; directory requirements may not.

distinctions.title: Substantive vs procedural ultra vires
distinctions.left: Content of the rule beyond legal power

misconceptions.trap: Only the parent Act matters; the Constitution is irrelevant to rules.
misconceptions.correction: Rules must also comply with the Constitution including fundamental rights.

misconceptions.trap: Any procedural slip voids a rule.
misconceptions.correction: Only mandatory procedural requirements have nullifying effect; directory requirements may not.

cases.name: In re Delhi Laws Act, 1912
cases.issue: What essential legislative functions cannot be delegated?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The legislature cannot surrender essential legislative functions; subsidiary details may be entrusted within policy and standard.

cases.name: State of Tamil Nadu v P. Krishnamurthy
cases.issue: On what grounds can subordinate rules be invalidated?
cases.ratioDecidendi: Subordinate legislation may be challenged for lack of competence, constitutional violation, failure to conform to the enabling Act, repugnancy and manifest arbitrariness.

cases.name: Indian Express Newspapers (Bombay) Pvt. Ltd. v Union of India
cases.facts: Delegated legislation imposing customs duty reviewed.
cases.issue: Does subordinate legislation enjoy the same immunity as plenary legislation?
cases.ratioDecidendi: Delegated legislation has no equivalent immunity and may be challenged for non-conformity with enabling statute and manifest arbitrariness.
cases.holding: Additional controls on subordinate legislation articulated.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a rulemaking-limits problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Test excessive delegation. II. Test substantive ultra vires. III. Test procedural ultra vires. IV. Test fundamental rights. V. Remedy (quash/sever).

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should submissions contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Parent Act; ground of invalidity; authorities already in file; precise relief.

examTips: List four limit families: delegation, substance, procedure, rights.
Separate procedural and substantive ultra vires.
Always start with the parent Act.
